speechtext: On the order being called for presenting reports:

subtopic: REPORT OF THE CLERK OF PETITIONS
speechtext:
Yesterday a question came up with regard to the report on a certain petition, and Objection was taken to the drafting of the report signed by Mr. Todd, who is the Examiner of Petitions. His report appears in the Votes and Proceedings of yesterday.
It was stated by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) that the examiner should not, so to speak, dictate to the House what course it should follow. I have read very carefully the report of Mr. Todd, who, by the way, has been almost fifty years in the service of parliament, and who is one of the most distinguished officials of this House. His report was not inspired by me, I need not say, and in my opinion Mr. Todd in presenting this report has followed what has been the practice of this House ever since my memory serves me.
Hon. members will see that Mr. Todd in his conclusions states:
The forai of this petition and its contents so far as the first part of the prayer is concerned are within the requirements of the 75th rule, and refer only to such matters as are within the right and competency of the House to deal with, should the House desire to do so; should, however, the course suggested in the second part of the prayer be taken by 'the House it would apparently have the effect of authorizing other persons to exercise a power which the House has already delegated by statute to the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts.
Apparently the first part of the prayer of this petition is only of a preliminary nature leading up to the main request as contained in the second part, consequently, the prayer, (considered as a whole, brings this petition within the rulling of Mr. Speaker Lemieux given on the 6th May last, in a somewhat similar case, which ruling was subsequently sustained by the House on appeal, viz., that a petition which prays for any action to be taken by the House that might involve in any respect an interference with the provisions of the Controverted Elections Act, chapter 7, R.S.C., 1906, cannot be received.
Under these circumstances I have therefore the honour to report that this petition should not be received.
Mr. Todd does not order the House, he does not even direct the House, not to receive the petition. He simply states that in his opinion, as an officer of fifty years' experience, and having always reported in that way to the House, the petition should not be received. But the House, of course, is at liberty to receive it or not, as it sees fit.	.

I should like to point out this, and I am not now dealing with the merits of this case at all: Last year on two occasions, on the 17th of June and again on the 27th of June the Clerk of Petitions reported on two different petitions with this postscript: "Irregular. Would involve the expenditure of public money." And in the House, on the 17th of June, and again on the 27th of June, Mr. Speaker decided, following the immemorial usage:
That as the granting of the prayer of this petition wouild involve the expenditure of public money, it cannot be received.
The same wording is used this year as last year; therefore there has been no departure in this case from the procedure followed in former days. It is taken as a matter of course that when this official makes his report, provided it is not in excess of his authority and that he keeps within the meaning of his prescribed duties, the House always accepts it. As I said a moment ago, I am not now speaking on the merits of this case. I notice there is a motion to reject the report and to proceed further with this petition.
As the action of this official was called in question yesterday, let me read from the Classification of the Civil Service of Canada, which defines his duties:
Olerk of Petitions
Definition of Class:
Under direction, to receive and handle petitions presented by members of the House of Commons; to read and revise petitions in accordance with the rules; to bring to the attention of the Speaker such petitions as do not comply with the rules and to point out their defects.
I respectfully submit that Mr. Todd only pointed out in his report to the House and to the Speaker the defects contained in this petition.
The standard authority in this House is Bourinot, who for half a century almost was our guide at the Clerk's table. He left before he died to the officials of this House his directions regarding the powers and privileges of the Houses of Parliament as respects their officers, clerks and servants, in which he says:
The Houses cannot part with any of these privileges, immunities and powers, necessary for the conduct of *business, their existence and their dignity, except by statute expressly conveying and delegating their powera, immunities and privileges to others. For instance, in the trial of controverted elections, the Commons parted with their jurisdiction previously exercised by committees of their own, and handed it over to judges in express terms.
I quote this simply to remind the House that Mr. Todd, who for a long period was associated with his immediate chief, Sir John Bourinot, could not ignore the principles and precedents laid down by the late Clerk. Some

Red Lake Railway Company
of those principles are to be found in a concrete form in section 91 of the Controverted Elections Act. But as I said a moment ago,
I am not passing on the merits of the case at all. This is a.temple of free speech and of free thought (in matters affecting parliamentary procedure. There is a motion to reject that report and it is within the right of the House to accept or reject it. I simply wish to present these considerations in justice to Mr. Todd and to point out that he did his duty, and only his duty, by reporting respectfully to the House his candid and honest opinion in regard to the petition.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a motion dealing with a private railway bill. May I just explain before I make the motion to refer this bill back to the select standing committee on Railways and Canals, that it is Bill No. 95, to incorporate the Red Lake and
Northwestern Railway Company. It came before the House some time ago and was sent to the Railway committee. When it came before that committee I was present so that if there appears to be-although there is not meant to be-any criticism in my words of the Railway committee, the criticism is as much of myself as of any other member of the committee. The bill has reference to a railway in northwestern Ontario, the section from which I come. I had never heard of the measure until it came before the committee and-I say this without disrespect to the committee in any way-we dealt with it rather briefly. I should like now, if the House will permit me, to make a motion referring the bill back to the committee. I have taken the matter up with some of the officers of the House and I am told that I am in order in doing so. The only thing I ask is that the bill be sent back to the committee. What becomes of it then is a matter for the committee to deal with; I am in no way concerned except in so far as it deals with a section of the country in which I am naturally interested, I therefore move, second by Mr. Lapierre, the hon. member for Nipissing:
That Bill No. 95, an act to incorporate the Red Lake and Northwestern Railway Company, :be referred back to the select standing committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines for reconsideration.
Speaking for a moment to the resolution, I wish to say that all I ask is that the committee have power to deal with the question again, because I am informed by those who are promoting the measure that they have information to give the committee at the present time which they did not give, or rather were not permitted to give, when the bill was last before the committee. I ask the House to allow the bill to go back to the Railway committee for them to deal with as they see fit. The section to be traversed by this projected line is a newly discovered mining district. It will probably mean great development for northwestern Ontario, and if the promoters of the enterprise can prove to the committee that this is a bona fide application for a charter with the intention of going on with the railway, and that they have the necessary financial support for the purpose of building this railway where no railway exists, it seems to me that the committee might well reconsider it. I am informed that the National Railways have no objection in any shape or form to this charter being given, but that is for the committee finally to deal with. I hope the House will permit this bill to go back to the committee for reconsideration.

Mr. Heenan was inaccurate in charging that the senator, as Minister of Labour, ordered into Winnipeg troops who fired on a crowd with fatal results. The only volleying that took place was (by the North West Mounted Police, forty-nine of whom were regularly stationed in the city.
Senator Robertson, on the other hand, was wrong in ihis statement that the only man shot was a foreigner who persisted dn throwing a missile after being warned by policemen. The red-coated "mo unties", after charging the mob several times, using clubs upon the scattering rioters, took up position dn front of the city jhaJll and on the word of command fired a volley with their revolvers. speechtext: When the bill was before the committee some days ago a question was raised as to the propriety of the proceedings in view of a mistake having been made in the single amendment comprising the reprinted bill. I promised to take the matter up with counsel, and I have ascertained from the Clerk of the House that the committee is in order in discussing the bill without reintroducing it inasmuch as the principle remains unchanged. All that has been altered is the wording of the amendment. My hon. friend (Mr. Boys) raised a question regarding the persons who are required to send in the report. We are seeking to amend section 41 of the Immigration Act which provides that upon certain offences being committed by aliens the board appointed by the minister for the hearing of such cases shall have authority, if necessary, to deport without trial before a court. We are now changing that regulation to provide for trial before the court; and upon conviction the immigration authorities shall undertake the deportation of the convicted persons. I think the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) wanted to know whether the offences remained. They do. I think I have answered all the points raised in the discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The discrimination was removed two years ago, I think.

It never was there to be removed. There never was any discrimination. I am not objecting to the clause being repealed. If I remember rightly a bill to repeal it was introduced by the late government in its last session-but failed in the Senate-on the ground merely that the circumstances which gave rise to the legislation and justified it no longer existed and that there was no need of keeping people in apprehension and unnecessary worry. But to assert that there was in it discrimination against the British bom is pure nonsense; there was nothing of the sort. The act provided that anybody coming to Canada- whether he was British-born or not did not matter-of the type and character described therein was subject to deportation. That is

to say, the discrimination in favour of the British-born which theretofore existed was removed as regards this class of people. If, for example, somebody came from France or from Italy of the type described in the act, he was subject to deportation upon inquiry before a board and proof that such was his character; but if a fellow came from somewhere in Scotland or England and was of just the same type, and was just the same menace to the country, there was no way of getting rid of him except by the formality of a trial. Under the circumstances of those times you could not do that. The minister, if he will take his mind back to those days, will recall that there was justification for this act. We did not impose any special discrimination against'the British-born immigrant at all; we removed something which was in his favour for the time being. I do not know that such a person would have very much to complain of if that enactment were allowed to stand. I do not know why an anarchist coming from Britain should be better treated than if he came from some other country. We ought to treat them all alike and give them all the same chance. But we do not want to encourage immigrants who believe in overthrowing government by force. For my part I would treat them all alike, whether British-born or natives of any other country. However, I do not think we are likely to get any of this type now, and I am not objecting to the repeal of the act.

to whom this would apply: The hon. member for East Edmonton was born in the Old Country and is not ashamed of it; my own colleague was born in England and I know he is not sahamed of it; the leader of the Progressive party was born in Scotland and I know he is not ashamed of it. If they were accused under the act as it now stands, the Acting Minister of Immigration and Colonization could have them before his committee and the day after to-morrow could ship them back to England, Ireland, or Scotland, as the case may be, without their having had any jury trial. Now, as a Canadian citizen I cannot be deported, but to me as a British subject, brought up in the idea of the liberty of the citizen and the right to trial by jury, that situation- which I venture to say most of the members have not realized1-is intolerable. We should insist that if any man comes to this country, whether from Great Britain or from some foreign land, and in this country commits or is alleged to have committed some crime, he ought to have a jury trial. I do not particularly object to his being deported if he is found guilty. Perhaps we made a mistake when this legislation was introduced earlier, because there were some hon. members in this chamber, and I think some in the other chamber, who got the idea that we wanted to retain these people in this country. That was not our thought at all, but we desired to get rid of obnoxious legislation which would permit deportation without trial by jury. I think the minister has fairly well met the situation by retaining the right of deportation, but providing that the deportation can take place only after conviction. I am sure there is not a member in this House who wants to deport anybody without trial. I can hardly conceive that any hon. member is willing to leave to a departmental committee the decision as to whether or not a man is guilty of offences of this kind. So it is quite clear that by the proposed amendment we refain the right to exclude undesirables or to deport people who prove to be of that class, but we do say that they should first have a fair trial. Surely that is fair.
Are they described in this clause?

No, and it is quite true that amendments to the Criminal Code are being proposed that will modify the legislation of 1919 regarding political crimes. But I would remind the hon. member that that has

nothing to do particularly with deportation. The Criminal Code does not provide for deportation. It provides for trial. We say that no one should be deported without trial.
That is not the true point.

There is no viewpoint in it. If the hon. member objects to the eliminations which are proposed in respect to the Criminal Code, the time to discuss the matter will be when they come up. I am quite willing to discuss them now, but I do not think it is the proper time. We will have an opportunity to discuss whether or not these emendations to the Criminal Code should be made, but that has nothing to do with deportation.

It has a very important bearing upon it, because some hon. members of this House might be perfectly willing to take some of these offences out of the Criminal Code and yet not to take them out of the Immigration Act. They might not be prepared to make those offences crimes under the Criminal Code; at the same time they might not want people of that character to be left in Canada.

Does the hon
member think he himself is in a very enviable position? Would he like his status to remain as it is, namely that he might be shipped out of the country without trial?

I am not dealing with that
point.
I am dealing with it.
My hon. friend is dealing with a point I have not rasied. He is - drawing a red herring across the trail.

No, I am trying
to keep to the point at issue.
I never raised that point.

This is a matter
of procedure, and in this bill we are making an effort to try to see that everyone who is living in Canada shall have the right to a jury trial. The question of deportation is a secondary matter. I am quite willing to concede that everyone in this country who commits any of these alleged crimes should be deported. I am not worrying about that part of it. Let them be kept out of the country, but after they are in the country let them have a fair trial so that it may be ascertained whether or not they are guilty.

Immigration Act

My hon. friend
has given a great deal of attention to this matter. He has referred to what is going to be done. Would he tell me what acts, hitherto looked upon as offences, are to be taken out of that category?

I am not against jury trial
or conviction, but section 97B is to be repealed by bill 153. That section says:
Any person who prints, publishes, edits, issues, circulates, sells, or offers for sale or distribution-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is not this bill.

I know that, but my hon.
friend says it is entirely a question of procedure. Either he 'has not appreciated what the bill provides for, or else he is not perfectly frank. This is a bill of procedure first, and secondly a bill of description of the particular acts that come within its terms. That element of the bill has been altered. I am not dealing with procedure. Leave that out. It is more than a bill of procedure when it changes the description of the acts which come under the deportable provisions of the law, and it changes those acts when it *-corporates the Criminal Code. The Minister of the Interior has been absolutely frank in respect to his answer to my question; he afterwards corrected himself and said, "I admit there are offences under the law as it now stands which will not be offences under the law after bill 153 is passed." For instance after the passing of bill 153 it will not be a deportable offence to print, publish, edit, issue circulate, sell or offer for sale or distribution any book, newspaper, periodical, pamphlet, picture, paper, circular, card, letter writing print, publication or document of any kind, in which is taught, advocated, advised or defended sedition.
Where do you find that?

That is section 97B of the
Criminal Code, part II, which will no longer be an offence if bill 153 is passed. Therefore a person who by word or act seeks to overthrow constitutional government, or advocates or suggests the unlawful destruction of property, will not be a deplorable subject after the Criminal Code amendment has gone through.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows
that that offence would come under some other section of the bill.

Not in part II. You wish not
to discuss this with bill 153, because palpably
the object of the government is to get this amendment through first, and having passed this, the other will be adopted also. I do not want this amendment to go through without the committee understanding what it is doing. If this amendment goes through and the Criminal Code amendment goes through the result will be that anybody can write or distribute literature and can work in any way along seditious lines for the overthrow of constitutional government in this country and advocate the destruction of property.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is going too far now, although his main argument is correct. My hon. friend is quoting from section 97 of the Criminal Code.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But does my hon. friend not forget that both section 41 of the Immigration Act and section 97B of the code were passed in 1919 for special reasons, all of which may have been good in themselves? I think he will find that the code in another section covers the point he is raising.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The man who would do what my hon. friend has read would come under section 132, which refers to seditious words, seditious libel, seditious conspiracy.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
All we are attempting to do in the Immigration Act by striking out the provisions of section 41 is to take from the control of the Minister of Immigration the power of deportation for offences of this character without trial. These provisions are not being struck out for the purpose of getting rid of these offences or of making them non-indictable offences. When we come to the amendment to the Criminal Code my hon. friend will be quite in order to raise the objections he is now raising, but I see no good purpose that will
Immigration Act

be served by delaying the taking away from the Minister of Immigration of the powers contained in section 41. Under section 40 the Minister of Immigration has all the power to deport without trial, but when this amendment goes through as regards the provisions contained in section 41 he will not have power to deport except after proper trial before a proper tribunal.
What are the powers in section 40?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They have always been in the Immigration Act. Section 40 reads:
Whenever any person, other than a Canadian citizen or person having Canadian domicile, shall be found an inmate of or connected with the management of a house of prostitution or practising prostitution, or who shall receive, share in, or derive benefit from any part of the earnings of any prostitute or who manages or is employed by, in, or in connection with any house of prostitution or music or dance hall or other place of amusement or resort habitually frequented by prostitutes, or where prostitutes gather, or who in any way assists any prostitute or protects or promises to protect from arrest any prostitute or who shall import or attempt to import any person for the purpose of prostitution or for any other immoral purpose, or who has been convicted of a criminal offence in Canada or who admits the commission prior to landing or entry to Canada of a crime involving moral turpitude, or has become a professional beggar or a public charge or practises polygamy, or has became an inmate of a penitentiary, gaol, reformatory, prison, asylum or hospital for the insane or the mentally deficient, or an inmate of a public charitable institution, or enters or remains in Canada contrary to any 'provision of this act, it shall be the duly of any officer cognizant thereof, and the duty of the derk, secretary or other official of any municipality in Canada wherein such person may be, to forthwith send a written complaint thereof to the minister, giving full particulars.

In those cases the minister will see that there are many things in respect to which the complaint may be made, and among them is conviction of a crime. The others do not include any conviction at all. The minister is capable of deporting in any such case upon evidence satisfactory to himself. Does that apply to anybody from Great Britain, or just to foreigners?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Any person who is not a Canadian.

That is just the point on fvhieh I want to make a remark. I do not know whether the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) can rest his soul in patience or not while section 40 stays within the act. I cannot understand how he can sleep at night. Think of it! Under that act men, women, by the score, by the hundred, can be deported without trial.
Why was it necessary to amend this in 1919?

To add another class who could be deported. What I am calling attention to is this: What seems to boil up in the soul of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is the idea of deporting anybody without trial. A jury trial, he says, is the right of a British subject. Still we have section 40 remaining under which in respect of 95 per cent of the cases there is no right to jury trial at all in determining whether the man or woman is deportable. This has been in the act for years. All that was done in 1919 was to add another class to those who were not entitled to jury trial. The class we added were those who came from the Old Country and were anarchists. In a word we added anarchists to prostitutes and beggars. That is all we did. We said: If a man was an anarchist, for the purpose of deportation he should not have any special rights merely because he came from Scotland or England. That was the terrible offence. It was not a case of invading the right to jury trial at all. The right to jury trial is the right of the citizen, whether he be a British subject or an Italian or a Swede or a Pole or a Jap.
This takes away that right.

No, it does not. The hon. member has never understood it. That right is a right that all have, British subject or no British subject, if they are living in Canada, before they can be punished for a crime. That is all that jury trial was ever intended for.
Will the hon. gentleman deny that the effort was made to deport men without trial?

The hon. member is in a hurry because I think he now sees the point. Jury trial is not anything that pertains to a British subject, to somebody born in Britain or Canada; it pertains to anybody before he is punished for a criminal offence. Under the code if he is charged with a major offence he has the right to jury trial. It is his right before he is punished for libel. But it is not anything that is especially the property of a British subject; it is just as much the property of a Pole or an African or a Hottentot. It never was the special right of anybody to have a jury trial before deportation. That is what I want to drive home to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. You do not need to establish crime against a man in order to have the right to deport him.

Immigration Act
Does the hon. gentleman think an Englishman who has been resident in this country for twenty years should be incapable of establishing Canadian domicile and be subject to deportation?

The hon. member is getting the red herring again; he is bound he will not follow me. For years he has been preaching before his own audiences that we took away the right of jury trial. We did not take it away at all. There never was the right of jury trial as a condition to deportation. That right exists only as a condition or protection against punishment for crime. I want to try to get that point into the hon. member's head.
Am I not right in arguing that the effect of such legislation would lead to the deprivation of such individuals of the right to trial by jury?
Just the same as the legislation that remains.
Quite so.

The hon. member is entirely satisfied, if some poor woman is found to be a prostitute, to deny her any right to jury trial, and to deport her. But if someone is found guilty of anarchism he immediately springs to his feet and espouses the right of that individual to trial by jury.
Who is to decide whether a person is guilty of anarchy?
The same person who decides whether some woman is guilty of prostitution.

I personally have taken the ground that it would be well to have legislation enacted providing that for all offences committed in Canada there should be trial by jury. But with regard to some of these cases the social effect of depriving the accused of that right is considerably greater, as in relation to political matters.

I am of the other view myself. I think there is a great deal more potential evil in some anarchists than in some poor girl who lives in a house of ill fame. The sympathies of the hon. gentleman are aroused only in the case of the anarchist, but he will not move a hand to repeal section 40.
As a matter of fact I have already moved in that direction. The hon. gentleman will find that four years ago I introduced legislation to repeal these sections.
Section 40?
Yes, that is my recollection.
It is not mine. I will not be positive-
That is my recollection.
-but as I remember, with respect to anarchists, the hon. gentleman's bill corresponded in effect to this legislation.
Would the right hon. gentleman consent to the repeal of section 40?

No; I would not. Not at all. And what is more, I do not see any special necessity for this bill. I do not think it is needed. What I am pointing out, however, is that the hon. member has for years misrepresented the legislation in this regard, and has got votes on that misrepresentation. He has never been fair about it; never in the world. This legislation merely put those who came from the Old Land, if they were found to be anarchists, on the same footing as immigrants from other countries who might be suspected of the same offence. It never denied them the right to trial by jury for the purposes for which trial by jury was instituted. Are hon. members going to say that it is tremendously important that merely because someone comes from the Old Land he must stay here, no matter what his character, even though he may be an anarchist, until you can get him convicted? Does any hon. member suggest that this should be the treatment accorded men coming from the Old Land and not men coming from Italy or France? Is it to be different in their case? I do not think that is fair.
Neither do I.

The hon. member agrees with me on that point when I mention the anarchist; but what interest does he display in behalf of offenders when I refer to other classes? Here is some fellow begging for a living; cannot find a job; throws himself upon public charity. The minister can deport him without any trial save such as he may himself conduct, and the plight of such an unfortunate does not seem to bother the hon. member at all. But if the minister undertakes to deport some man on the ground of his being an anarchist, then woe betide the government! This, briefly, is the stand the hon. member takes.
Immigration Act

It is difficult to tell just
what this debate is all about. One does not know whether it is a discussion of the Winnipeg strike or a consideration of the Immigration Act. But it seems to me that the Winnipeg strike is one cogent reason why section 41 of the act of 1919 should be retained on the statute books. I certainly do not think the repeal of that act can be justified. Every loyal citizen of this Dominion sympathized with the government when it passed section 41 which hon. gentlemen are endeavouring so strenuously to-day to repeal. Do those hon. gentlemen want us to revert to the appalling conditions that prevailed in 1919 and prior to that time?
The responsibility for maintaining law and order is a very serious one, and it is all that our police systems in Canada can do to keep the peace. This is distinctly a retrograde step. It is one which the people in the country will not regard favourably. Australia has refused to loosen up on its law in regard to immigrants who commit offences that make them liable to deportation. Look at the strike that occurred in the Old Country the other day: what was responsible for it? It was the result of propaganda, and the same sentiments that led to that strike are so rampant in this country at the present time that those in authority who are responsible for the maintenance of law and order find their duties exceedingly difficult. I do not care whether the agitator is a British subject or not; if he does not abide by the law he should be deported be he Greek, Jew, or Gentile. The sooner this country wakes up and puts on the statute books a proper law, and one sufficiently stringent, the better it will be for administration generally and for law and order in the country.
I am absolutely opposed to this change, for which there is no demand that I can see. The civil authorities whose business it is to keep order have not asked for it. As a matter of fact, the municipalities are very largely against it, and the police themselves are opposed to it. They discussed the question at a convention in Ottawa some time ago, and while I cannot speak for them I think I am safe in saying that as a unit they took a stand against any interference with the immigration law as it was adopted in 1919. No one who is liable to deportation, whether he be a British subject or not, should be immune from the provisions of the act. And some of the most dangerous agitators in Canada today, some of whom I know myself, come from the British Isles. The average foreigner

is peaceable and law-abiding, and he tries to obey the laws of the land; but some of these agitators bring with them into Canada views of government which are not shared for a moment by the people here who have built up this country. There should be no special provision for the British subject if he is an agitator or an anarchist. He should be treated just like any ether undesirable. These disturbers of the peace advocate policies that are the reverse of good government. With the experience which the government have gained during the past four years, and in the light of the Winnipeg strike, the labour troubles that have prevailed in the Maritime provinces, and the industrial unrest generally, not only in this country but elsewhere as well, notably in the Motherland and in Australia, I fail to see how hon. gentlemen opposite could bring down a bill like this and seriously ask parliament to adopt it. It is not too late to withdraw the bill and I hope the government will see fit to do so.
When agitation was rife in the Australian Commonwealth what did Premier Bruce say? He'said: "We will make this a white man's country. It does not matter whether the anarchist came from Europe or from the British Isles, he will be deported. Everyone who comes to this country has got to abide by the law and if he attempts to make any disturbance we will deport him." That is the attitude taken by the premier and the government of Australia, and that is the attitude we should take in this country. The Australian parliament backed up Premier Bruce by an overwhelming majority. I have come across a good many agitators in my time. When I was chairman of the Board of Police Commissioners in Toronto the board had frequently to consider cases of disturbance created by men of this type. I remember on one occasion there was a good deal of trouble, and the foreigners in St. John's ward were by no means to blame.
The government will have to take the responsibility for any violations of the law to whiefh this legislation may give rise. The responsibility is on their shoulders. T. know of no reason why agitators who are British by naturalization should not be subject to the same deportation laws when they try to upset constituted government, and cause trouble in Canada. On the government of the day is the responsibility for maintaining law and order. In the British House of Commons the Right Hon. Sir John Simon recently declared himself strongly against the doctrines of communism as subversive of the state, and

Red Cross Society Act
expressed the opinion that in the last resort the Attorney General should prosecute whoever disseminated such doctrines. I agree with him. Colonel Grassett, a former chief of police of Toronto, on one occasion expressed the opinion that it is better to let agitators hold their meetings in the open rather than have them disseminate their noxious doctrines in secret meetings. The time has come when something should be done to regulate communism in this country. To-day there are Sunday schools in Toronto where communists are teaching their children these continental European doctrines -doctrines which are not British and are alien to the soil of Canada. It is the duty of the government to check such teaching. I believe in proper support for labour, but I venture to say that the real labour leaders of Canada do not approve of communism; they respect British institutions.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that it is a retrograde step on the part of the government to introduce this bill. Section 41 of the act of 1919 is a very good section, and you might as well abolish the immigration officers altogether if you are not going to strengthen their hands in the larger centres of population. In this matter we should take a leaf out of the book of the United States. When the government of that country found a few years ago that Americans of Anglo-Saxon stock would soon be in a minority, they passed what is popularly known as the quota law, which limits the annual number of immigrants from any country. One thing you must respect the Americans for-they make everyone obey the laws. I repeat it is a retrograde step to repeal section 41 and substitute this section, which means nothing. I contend-*

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It now being six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I ask that the committee rise and report progress.

Before the committee rises, will not the minister admit that under the law as it stands the power of deportation applies only to a British immigrant during the first five years of his residence in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, once they become citizens you cannot deport them.
And they become citizens in five years or three?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Five years is the shortest period.

In that connection, is it not. true that a man mav remain
in Canada' six, eight or ten years without taking out papers-I know some do-and then be deported?
That does not apply here at all; that man is not a British subject. Once a British subject has been in Canada for five years the act does not apply.

No one, according to the act, who belongs to the prohibited or undesirable classes within the meaning of section 41 shall be capable of acquiring Canadian domicile, and then the act proceeds to enumerate the classes of undesirables. So it does not make any difference whether such an immigrant is here for five years cr twenty, he cannot acquire Canadian domicile.

That cannot be the effect, as is shown by the discussion in 1923
Progress reported.

maintopic: CANADIAN RED CROSS SOCIETY ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext:
Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence) moved the second reading of Bill No. 151, to amend the Canadian Red Cross Society Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Duff in the chair.
On section 1-Disposal of property.

maintopic: CANADIAN RED CROSS SOCIETY ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
What is the object of
this bill?

maintopic: CANADIAN RED CROSS SOCIETY ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I explained the purpose of this bill on the first reading. Under the act of 1909 incorporating the Red Cross Society, which was consolidated under the legislation of 1922, power was given to the Red Cross Society to hold and acquire property for the purposes of the society, but strangely enough, no power was given to the society to dispose of their property when they should find it necessary or advisable to do so. During the war, I am instructed by Doctor Robertson, who is head of the Red Cross Society, in different parts of the country the society acquired little pieces of property which in their own interests they desire to dispose of from time to time, and this bill simply gives them power to dispose of it as they see fit
Railway Act Am'endment

maintopic: CANADIAN RED CROSS SOCIETY ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The same
power as is enjoyed by other societies?

maintopic: CANADIAN RED CROSS SOCIETY ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Yes.
There is nothing more involved in the bill than that.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and
passed.

Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved the second reading of Bill No. 149, to amend the Railway Act, 1919.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Duff in the chair.
On section 1-Apportionment of money of railway grade crossing fund.

We have had a very full discussion of this measure, but I think there is just one thing the minister was going to look into. It was the point raised by the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary). Has my hon. friend looked into that?

I have made some inquiries regarding the matter, more especially of the Board of Railway Commissioners, because of course their past practice with regard to this matter is important. I am informed that it has been the practice of the board to interpret section 262 liberally, and that following such practice each separation of grade-that is, each particular crossing of a highway by a railway, or vice versa, even though a number of such crossings be included in one work or project ordered by the board-would be treated as a crossing within the definition of the same in the act, and aid therefore could in each case be apportioned to the extent of 25 per cent of the cost thereof not exceeding $15,000, subject to the limitations in the act respecting the number of crossings in each municipality. That is the manner in which the board has administered the old provision, and I think it clears up the point.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

Hon. GEORGE H. BOIVIN (for the Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 114, to amend the Customs Tariff, 1907.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Duff in the chair.
On section 1-British preferential tariff.

I suppose this
relates entirely to the West India treaty, does it not? No, it has to do with our own ports.
Yes, itr limits the preference to our own ports.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Schedule A amended.

I think this
very largely refers to the West India treaty, does it not?
Clause 2 contains the general changes. Of course some of these changes refer to the West India treaty.
I think we have an understanding with the Minister of Finance to the effect that these changes in connection with the West India treaty shall not come into force until the treaty is ratified.

I believe that understanding is perfectly correct, with the exception of a slight amendment with respect to cocoa beans.
Before section 2 carries I beg to move an amendment to tariff item 626a, namely, that the enumeration of goods and the several rates of duties set opposite that item be struck out. This change was asked for by the maufacturers of men's and boys' hats in Canada who imported the hoods in the rough from foreign countries. It will be remembered that a slight change was made when the resolution was before the committee to meet the requests of certain Canadian manufacturers of the same kind of hoods. After that change was made and the bill was printed the manufacturers of hats who do not manufacture hoods represented to the government that they were being placed in a worse position than before. The striking out of tariff item 626a leaves the customs tariff absolutely as it was before and there is no change whatever in that regard.

The item is
just dropped.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 3-Schedule B amended.

In regard to section 1055
there has been a request made to alter very

Customs Tariff
slightly the wording, and instead of using the words "when used in the manufacture of" in the first line, substitute the words "which enter into the cost of". Certain manufacturers in Canada represent to us that they must procure oil's and machinery for the manufacture of these parts; that if they are not placed in the same proportionate relation to the imported parts as they are at the present time they will suffer hardship, and that therefore the machinery, oil and other materials required for the manufacture of these parts should be subject to the same drawback a3 the part itself, when it is imported by the Canadian manufacturer.
Does that include the dies?
Yes.

All machines
used in the manufacture of automobile parts?
Yes, they will be subject to the 25 per cent drawback upon the present rate of duty.
You should make it read, "All machines used in the manufacture of automobiles," because you cannot make automobiles without using parts.
Yes, it would apply to both.
How many of these machines are at present made in Canada, dies and the like?

I am not in a position to give that information, although I am told that the stamping machines are not manufactured in Canada at all at present, and it is precisely to cover the very expensive stamping machines that we are asked to make this amendment.
It is not limited to stamping machines?

No. It is to cover all machinery used in the manufacture of the parts which may be imported into Canada with the 25 per cent drawback. The manufacturers of parts and the manufacturers of automobiles represent that if they are obliged to pay full rate of duty on the machinery which they must import they will be suffering a hardship of 25 per cent, and that they should enjoy the same proportionate advantage as the company manufacturing parts in the United States.

It hardly does that. I think the minister means that he puts them, having regard to the capital account necessary for their machinery and machinery
supplies, in the same position as they are having regard to the drawback on the finished article.

It has been stated in the
department that if we leave in the section the words "when used in the manufacture of," it will mean the actual material which goes into the car itself, and that it would be clearer to substitute the words, "which enter into the cost of".
I apprehend from what the minister says, that all machinery used in the manufacture of automobiles is now to go on the free list.

Oh, by no means. A great deal of it comes in at 27J per cent duty and perhaps more. This amendment would give a reduction of 25 per cent on the present rate of duty. In other words, the present rate of duty would be reduced by one-quarter when the machinery is used exclusively in the manufacture of automobiles.
How are you going to protect the manufacturer of machinery fpr that loss of protection? Are you going to put him in the position he was in before?

That is one of the difficulties of an intricate protective tariff, but the representations made to the government have been that the drawback clause would cause serious hardship to the manufacturers supplying parts to those car manufacturers who are now making 75 or 85 per cent of their car in Canada. If they could purchase the excess of the 40 or 50 per cent of their car, which must be of Canadian manufacture, in the United States cheaper than they could purchase the same parts here, they would naturally give the preference to the American market. In order to place the Canadian manufacturer of parts in a position to meet as far as possible that reduction of 25 per cent, it is only fair to give him a reduction of 25 per cent of the duty on his machinery. It is true, as the hon. member pointed out, that there may be a slight hardship in this for the manufacturers of machinery, but it must be remembered that they are not manufacturers of machinery for the purposes of the manufacture of automobiles only; that they have a very wide range of factories to which they can sell that machinery, and their loss of protection will only be one-quarter of the present rate of duty on machinery sold to the automobile manufacturers.

I am thoroughly aware
of that, but it means you are cutting away

My hon. friend is quite

Of course one

Last year we imported something like $11,000,000 worth of steel for agricultural implements and it is safe to say that a good deal of that steel was used for something which was not strictly an agricultural implement. The steel companies have always complained that you cannot police this matter. We are getting more and more into that policy. My hon. friend is right; he cannot help it. The trouble is that the government started by laying down a policy and made some cuts without knowing anything about the matter. In that way they have caused a great deal of trouble and they are now trying to fix up their fences. It is a natural thing to endeavour to correct the harm we do particularly when the inevitable results unless we do that are shown.
My hon. friend ought not to think that the manufacturers of parts have a protective duty of 30 to 35 per cent on automobiles, because he knows that a very large proportion of automobiles are exported and there is a large rebate of duty on exports. The result is that if a manufacturer is exporting 50 per cent of his output, as regards his cost in purchasing parts the duty of 30 per cent on his parts drops down on his total business to 15 per cent. I think my hon. friend will follow me in that. As the matter now stands, that actual duty of 15 per cent, although an apparent duty of 30 per cent, will under this change become a duty of something like 11 per cent, or one-quarter off fifteen.
The export is about 47 per cent.

Under this item practically everything that goes into a machine shop, engines, boilers, lathes, drills, shears, shafting, boxes equipment of every description, will be subject to the drawback of 25 per cent in the duty. It means simply that a manufacturer of machinery of every description is going to be penalized to this extent. This is a case of endeavouring to transfer the burden from one man to another. There is not a manufacturer of machinery in this country who is not going to be hurt to that extent under this clause.

If my hon. friends seriously object to the amendment I do not want to

To start in this piecemeal business of attacking first one industry and then another and then to try to rectify something that should not have been done is not the way to proceed at all. Before the motion is carried I should like to have from the government a statement of its policy in relation to the despatch of troops into strike areas. In this conection I want to relate some of the circumstances that attended the strike in Winnipeg in 1919. On March 11 I stated on the floor of this House that troops had been sent into Winnipeg at the time of that strike, that shots were fired, and that a person was killed; and I added that had the then Minister of Labour exercised a little horse sense that strike could have been settled without any bloodshed. Now I desire to prove these statements.
I notice that the ex-Minister of Labour, speaking in another place, lamented the fact that he had left the files behind him when he left the department, but I want to assure him that the files are all right. They are intact, and to refresh his memory I shall quote

several of his own telegrams and communications as taken from those very files. The strike occurred on May 15, 1919 and I find that on the previous day, May 14, General Kitchen, the commanding officer in Winnipeg, communicated with the secretary of the military council at Ottawa, advising that the mayor of Winnipeg had communicated to him his intention of calling upon the military authorities to take steps to protect property. So that we have evidence there that it was the intention of the mayor to seek the assistance of the military authorities.
On May 19, four days after the strike was declared, General Kitchen wired from Winnipeg to Military Headquarters at Ottawa:
At the request of the mayor and on his written statement that he anticipated disturbances beyond the powers of oivil authorities to deal with, a percentage of the active militia 'has been called out.
In that comunication he enumerated the different battalions, eleven in number. So that right at the outset we have evidence that the militia had been called out. On the 15th of the month, the day the strike took place, instructions were sent for a squadron of the Northwest Mounted Police returning from overseas, to be demobilized at Winnipeg and handed over to Commissioner Perry. Later this was done. Consequently during their term of duty in Winnipeg they were members of the mounted police and not of the Canadian Expeditionary Force. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the authorities were camouflaging and pretending that these men of the Canadian Expeditionary Force were members of the mounted police because of the fact that they had been demobilized-and for a purpose.
On May 20 General Kitchen wired for authority as to the source of pay for the militia units that he had called out or of the portion of the units that might be used in the course of the strike. On the same day he was advised that the pay would come from the military authorities.
On May 22 the Adjutant General sent a message to General Kitchen that the Hon. Mr. Meighen and Senator Robertson were convinced by the Citizens Committee lof Winnipeg that a certain officer at the head of the militia should be relieved and his place taken by some other officers whose names they suggested. On the same date a message was sent by General Kitchen to the acting prime minister and the military authorities at Ottawa reporting that everything was quiet in Winnipeg, that there were no signs of disturbance, but asking that extra Lewis guns be furnished and forwarded to Winnipeg under guard. It rather looked as if everything was not so quiet.

Supply-Winnipeg Strike
On May 23 General Hill was ordered to go to Montreal to meet the 27th battalion, explain the situation at Winnipeg, and ascertain whether the whole or a portion of that battalion would consent to remain on duty during the period of emergency in Winnipeg. He was also advised that an officer would report to him at Turcotte yards, near Montreal, at 3.30 a.m. on the 24th instant with eight Lewis machine guns packed in ordinary packing boxes and marked regimental baggage, 27th Battalion." These were to be placed on the first train carrying that unit and delivered to the officer commanding military district No. 10 on arrival. The message continued:
An officer will deliver twelve Lewis guns similarly packed and addressed at Smiths Falls on arrival of the first train. It is desired that these guns reach Winnipeg without anyone being the wiser.
If the then Minister of Labour did not know what was going on he should have known, because his government was doing this.
On May 25 Senator Robertson wired for the information of council that in his judgment:
This is not an opportune time to make a declaration in favour of principle collective bargaining as it [DOT]would be grasped as an excuse by strikers to claim they have forced the government and thereby proved success of sympathetic strike.
In the same message he added:
I anticipate that the general strike will either be called off very shortly or a last desperate move made to make it successful. If it proves a failure the One Big Union movement intended to be launched at the Calgary convention on June 4-
That is, about ten days ahead.
-will I think also fail. These are my personal views expressed in Mr. Meighen's absence and for the information of council.
I said the other day, Mr. Speaker, that had the then Minister of Labour used a little horse sense the strike could have been settled without bloodshed. The strike was called on May 15, and everyone that had anything to do with it said that it was for the purpose of maintaining the principle of collective bargaining. Yet on May 25-ten days afterwards- it appears that some of his colleagues in council here had been advising him to make a declaration in favour of the principle of collective bargaining, but Senator Robertson at the time apparently put his own views before those of some of his colleagues and said that this was not the proper time to make such a declaration. His only excuse was that he was afraid the strikers would be encouraged to prolong the strike. I submit that right there and then he had the greatest opportunity of his life, either to call the bluff 14011-254
of the strikers if he thought they were bluffing, or to settle the strike; but he failed to do so.
On May 26 General Kitchen reported the arrival of the 27th battalion in Winnipeg, and that he was conferring with General Hill that evening. He added:
The machine gun section was in serviceable condition.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the ex-Minister of Labour in another place stated that on his honour as a minister of the crown there was not one soldier sent into Winnipeg. Well, there we have the acknowledgment of the arrival of the 27th battalion with twenty Lewis machine guns. I do not know bow he harmonizes those two conflicting statements.
On May 26 General Kitchen communicated with the Prime Minister and others that after conferring with the ministers who were in Winnipeg-that is, Senator Robertson and Mr. Meighen-the only solution to his mind was to have the agitative leaders arrested for instigation and intimidation. He continued:
If this was possible I consider the bottom would fall out of the movement to tie up the whole country by
a sympathetic strike.
On May 27 Senator Robertson again wired council that labour leaders were frantically endeavouring to camouflage the issue by attempting to contend for the recognition of collective bargaining, and that "General Kitchen's arrangements were both adequate and admirable." In the first place, he had refused to make a declaration in favour of tne principle of collective bargaining, and two or three days afterwards he pointed out that the strike leaders were camouflaging, yet he did not use enough horse sense to call their bluff. So I repeat my statement that had he used a little horse sense he could have settled the strike without one shot being fired and without any bloodshed.
On May 31 General Kitchen wrote to the Minister of Justice, that Mr. Meighen, and Senator Robertson had arrived in Winnipeg on May 22, and that Mr. Meighen had issued a proclamation to the postal service on strike warning them that all employees would be given until 11 a.m. on the 26th of May to return to duty, that after that date such as did not accept the offer would be dismissed and debarred from further employment in the postal service, and that the vacancies so caused would be immediately filled by 9 p.m. the selection of suitable volunteers.. During the last election, Mr. Speaker, the late Minister of Labour, Mr. Murdock, was very properly ridiculed for

Supply-Winnipeg Strike

telling the post office employees at Toronto "They could stay out until hell froze over." This is a similar expression, in effect that if they did not accept the position by a certain date they could also stay out till the same place had frozen over.
Then there was a certain time which was apparently utilized to beat the strikers rather than to settle the strike. On June 5th, Senator Robertson wrote a letter giving permission for 44 porters to be brought in from the United States to take the place of the Canadian Pacific Railway men on strike. On June 7th, Mr. Andrews of Winnipeg, who was acting for the Justice department, wired Senator Robertson giving details of an offer of the metal employers to settle the strike. Here was an opportunity to settle the strike at the instance of the employers themselves.
On June 9th a message was sent by a gentleman who I understand was a member of this House at that time, Mr. Allan, interfering in the matter. He wired to a gentleman by the name of Nanton-I think we all knew Sir Augustus Nanton-as follows:
Feel strongly company should adhere to refusal mediator's proposal collective bargaining and that sympathetic strike should be called off before negotiations are resumed. Understand citizens' committee and companies agreed sympathy strike cannot be allowed wholly or partially to succeed.
In other words, they were more interested in breaking the strike than in settling the strike. Evidently the interference had some result, because on June Kith Sir Augustus Nanton answered Mr. Allan-and by the way, through the military sources here-to the effect that all sympathetic strikes must be called off as a preliminary to any further negotiations, and Senator Robertson was again called on to use all his influence in the matter.
On June 9th evidently there were some members of the government here at Ottawa who did not desire the strike should be called off, because I find here a message from Mr. Meighen to Mr. Andrews advising that certain legislation was likely to be introduced- we were discussing some of that legislation today-and it seemed to him-Mr. Meighen- that the settlement on the terms proposed would be a triumph for the strike leaders. In other words, members of the government here ait Ottawa were not anxious that the strike should be settled or that the plans the employers had submitted should be accepted.
On June 15th, Senator Robertson wired the Prime Minister that owing to the failure of mediation proceedings and the strike extending to the train service men a clear-cut definition and declaration on the question of colfMr. Heenan.]
lective bargaining seemed to be justified, and that such was submitted to the metal trade employers and had been accepted. After he had refused to make this declaration on May 25th, he now considers, on June 15th, that this is the opportune time to make the statement he should have made I'ong before. He advised further in that telegram that further action outlined in the telegram of the 13th was likely to be taken within the next twenty-four hours, "which we anticipate will result in speedy and satisfactory conclusion of the trouble here." In other words, he was advising that there, would be arrests of some of the men within the next twenty-four hours, and within the next twenty-four hours ten men were arrested.
On June 17th, Senator Robertson wired the Prime- Minister pointing out the importance of providing machinery for the deportation of undesirables, also advising him of ten arrests on the previous night, and that the Labour temple and several Labour hal'ls had been searched for printed literature and records.
On June 17th, the day after the arrests, Mr. Meighen wired from Ottawa to Mr. Andrews in Winnipeg questioning the legality of the arrests, and pointing out that the arrests had been made without proper authorization, but that the proper authorization was being immediately despatched. In other words, the men -had been arrested illegally, but once arrested the government was going to make their arrests legal. Mr. Andrews got a slight slap on the wrist there from (Mr. Meighen), and answering the Minister the next day he practically blamed the whole situation on Senator Robertson. He said:
Everything I have done has been at the suggestion of Senator Robertson, but because it might weaken his position with Labour I have taken the full responsibility for the Justice department.
In other words, Senator Robertson was in politics, and if he had done anything along these lines it might have weakened his position with Labour if it had been found out, so they had in Winnipeg, acting for the Justice department, another gentleman, who was not in politics, and who took full responsibility in order to save Senator Robertson in a political way.
On June 17th Mr. Meighen wired to Mr. Andrews that although he had himself questioned the legality of what had been done, it was all right anyway. He said:
Notwithstanding any douibt I have as to the technical legality of the arrest and the detention at Stony Mountain, I feel that rapid deportation is the best course now that the arrests are made, and later we can consider ratification.

Supply-Winvipeg Strike
In other words, legal or not, the arrests had been made and the government were determined to get these men out of the country, and later ratify the action that had been taken. We were discussing a bill here this afternoon, in a camouflaged sort of way which does not go to the kernel of the matter, for the legislation was put there for no other purpose than to break the strike in 1919.
On June 17th Mr. Calder wired to the head of the mounted police in Winnipeg:
You are 'hereby authorized under section 42 of the Immigration Act to take into custody and detain for examination for the purposes of deportation the several persons referred to in your telegram of the seventeenth.
In that he was authorizing the arrest and detention of men after they had already been arrested and detained in Stony Mountain.
Again, on the same day Mr. Meighen wired to Senator Robertson advising delay in arrests, in which he said that the provincial government had so advised. "Authorization depends wholly on you." In other words, Senator Robertson was in Winnipeg with full authority in regard to the arrests, but in view of the fact that the provincial government advised against	the arrests	Mr.	Meighen wired	toSenator	Robertson	that authorization	depended wholly upon him, the Minister of Labour. On the same date Mr. Calder wired to Judge Robson as follows:
Message received. If Senator Robertson has not left, please get in touch with him immediately as local representative was directed, to obtain his approval for any action contemplated.
Again putting the whole responsibility on Senator	Robertson,	the	then Minister	ofLabour.	On June	18th	Senator Robertson
wired the Prime Minister reporting: everything quiet in Winnipeg and that "our action has proved effective and satisfactory to citizens generally and will be wholly justified." He asked in the same message that certain amendments to the Criminal Code be hastened, as Commissioner Perry, of the northwest mounted police, might desire to take general action throughout western Canada at an early date. Having arrested ten men illegally and put them in Stony Mountain penitentiary, having conquered Winnipeg, as it were, he was now prepared to attack the whole of western Canada. He therefore asked for certain legislation to be hastened so that he could get out on the war path again. On June 19 the Prime Minister wired Senator Robertson as follows:
Thanks for various messages and especially your telegram of yesterday. Pray accept warmest congratulations upon your masterly handling of a very difficult and complicated situation.

So that apparently the whole proceedings had the blessing of the Prime Minister and the government generally. But two days later something serious happened. I have led up to the point where a situation occurred that is deplorable to think of. On June 21st a message was received here in Ottawa to this effect:
Serious riot started at 2.45 p.m. Mounted police turned out and now engaged with crowd. Mayor read Riot Act and called on militia. Turning out at once.
So it happened that the militia were used. On the same day there was a message from Mr. Andrews to Hon. Mr. Meighen in reference to the strike, in which he stated:
I think, however, if we had not admitted to bail riots would have 'been participated in by strike committee who I believe, did all in their power to prevent red soldiers parade which started riot.
I want to draw this to the attention of hon. members: The strike committee were blamed for causing a riot. The ex-Minister of Labour, speaking in another place on the 12th of May, went on to say that the committee of the strikers with whom he had been negotiating at an hotel left the hotel with the statement that they were going out to fight that afternoon, and one of them said, "No, we don't want anything to eat; we can fight better on an empty stomach." Nevertheless we find the general officer commanding in Winnipeg making this statement in a telegram to the Hon. Mr. Meighen: "I believe the strike committee did all in their power to prevent the red soldier parade which started the riot." On the other hand Senator Robertson is found declaring in another place that the strike committee were prepared to fight on empty stomachs.

In the riots the hon.
member speaks of were any people killed?
Yes.
How many?
One.

Were there any others
killed during the strike in addition to that one person?

Not that I know of. I
do not mind any hon. gentleman asking questions. May I say just at this point that I was in Winnipeg. I have been in the labour movement all my life, and have been at the head of every union with which I have been identified locally and I never was on strike one day in my life. I was more interested in an honourable settlement of this strike at that time than I was in anything else. But when it comes down to placing the respon-
Supply-Winnipcc Strike

sibility for certain occurrences that took place at that time I am going to state the facts no matter who is injured by it.
Senator Robertson in another place made the assertion that I had made a false statement on the floor of this House knowing it to be false, and that I did so for a malicious purpose.
My hon. friend has invited questions; may I ask him one more? Was it the troops or the mounted police that did the killing?

If my hon. friend had
been following me he would have gathered that a squadron of mounted police arriving from overseas had been demobilized in Winnipeg so that they would not be known as soldiers but as mounted police. They were the men that did the shooting. If my hon. friend will just give me time I will cover all those points as I go along.

What do you
hope to accomplish by rehashing this" matter of the Winnipeg strike? You are simply creating bad feeling in this country.

I hope to vindicate my
honour in the face of the charges made against me.

It was nothing
but an attempt at revolution, that is all it was.

On what do you base
that opinion?
Mr. SPENCE (Parkdale); Everybody is of that opinion.

I will tell you what it
was: A straw man was simply put up for the purpose of knocking it down. That is all it was. I never heard anything so ridiculous in my life as the suggestion that there was an attempt at revolution in Winnipeg. The 27th battalion with twenty machine guns were there, and yet the ex-Minister of Labour made the statement in another place that not one soldier was called upon. This is the gentleman who charged an hon. member of this House with making a malicious statement knowing it to be false. Do hon. gentlemen opposite think that I have no honour or selfrespect?
The ex-Minister of Labour in another place made a statement to the effect that there were men on the tops of buildings and other very secluded places firing rifle or revolver shots at the mounted police. There is on record a report from one of his own men who states

the circumstances under which the shots were fired. I cannot pronounce this man's name, no Irishman in this country could pronounce it. The initial of his Christian name is all right. It is "P". Whether that is "Patrick" or not, I do not know. The surname is spelled in the following manner- G-U"g-e-y-e-z-u-c-k.
Can you sneeze it?

The ex-Minister of Labour eulogizes this individual in another document as one who could be depended upon and recommends that he be given extra pay for his work during the trouble. This man had been reporting regularly. Two days after the strike, on the 23rd of May. he states:
The authorities were well prepared to stop any disturbance. At 2.30 they began to gather around the market square. The Royal Northwest Mounted Police and special police came up to keep order and stop the parade. As soon as they were near the crowd many stones and bricks were thrown at them and yelling "boo-hoo". In reply to this the mounted police started shooting. There was one killed, thirty were injured and about one hundred arrested.
Instead of firing revolver shots from the tops of buildings, as the senator says, somebody shouted "boo-hoo". Then the mounted police started shooting and1 killed a man.
They did fire a revolver shot and threw two brickbats. I was there myself at the time.

What is the government doing in this connection? I ask the government to amend the act so that no soldiers can be sent into any strike area, except on the responsibility of the government. I do not believe we should allow orders to go round this country promiscuously, requiring soldiers to go into any of these areas. I think I have proved conclusively that the Minister of Labour did on a whim of his own, against the advice of some of his own colleagues, prolong the strike by refusing 'to declare in favour of collective bargaining. I think he says himself it was in the interests of the international unions. Speaking in another place the hon. minister said that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, who was a young member in the House, should confess his indiscretion in making such statements, should admit the truth and thus apologize. In speaking to the House I have left out a lot of quotations from statements from the files because I think it is in the interest of the country not to use them.
In conclusion I have one apology to make, and that is that I was one of the men who was instrumental in recommending to the Prime Minister the appointment of Senator

Supply-Winnipeg Strike
Robertson to represent Labour in the Senate of Canada. I have now to apologize and say that we appointed a man who became a misfit, and through his indifference actually caused the riots in Winnipeg. I repeat again that he used a little common sense-
Order, order.

I would remind the hon. member that the gentleman of whom he is speaking is a member of the Senate. According to our rules decorum must be observed and no expression imputing discredit on a member of the House of Commons or member of the Senate should be used. The hon. member used the expression u misfit and applied it to a senator. I do not think the expression is parliamentary, and I ask the hon. member to withdraw it.
Mr. IiEENAN: I withdraw it; I am sorry I used it if it is against the rules. But I think someone should communicate to the other chamber and inform them of the rule, so that the same order might prevail over there. I do not think a member of the House of Commons, who has to go before the electors, should be spoken about in the way I was spoken about by a member of the Senate who feels a certain amount of security, ;n that he does not have to face the electors. 1 do not want to dictate to the Speaker, but I feel that in all fairness he should communicate to the Speaker of the Senate the ruling he has just given. I am perfectly -willing to abide by it. The ruling is a proper one.
The strike we have been discussing should have been settled, but the whole negotiation leading up to the riot was carried on in a manner to prevent its being settled. I do not think anyone could rely on the information the commanding officer was receiving from different sources, because I find in the documents that he had secured a man to go amongst the labour unions as one of them, to find out what was going on and report to the officer. He was paid $75 a week on account of the danger of the job. But, hon. members will note that the officer had so little confidence in that man that he had to employ another man at $50 a week to check him up for fear he would be double-crossed. That is the report received from the general officer commanding at Winnipeg. If I had been an officer of the crown receiving the reports here, I would have been afraid there was actually a revolution of some description in progress in Winnipeg. I say there was no sign of a revolution, and when the minister went up there for the purpose of settling the matter, if he had really attempted to settle it or was desirous of settling it, he
could have done so without the delay that actually did occur in bringing about a settlement.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):

speechtext: In explanation I may say that I said I would take it up at the first opportunity.

I did not know what
would be the hon. member's first opportunity,, consequently I am in -the position of nob knowing precisely what the hon. member's words were. As I went to Winnipeg at the time with the Minister of Labour of that day, and had to do with all with which the Minister of Labour had to do, I am tolerably familiar with the circumstances, and in referring to those circumstances, speak only under the handicap of the time which has since elapsed.
I have just had the opportunity of reading what was said in another place by the Minister of Labour at that time. Only now have I had the time to read it, and I hasten to say that what was said by the Minister of Labour in another place was, in every line of it, correct. No troops whatever were ordered into Winnipeg by the government or anybody else at the time of the strike in 1919. Not only were none ordered in. but none went in and none had anything to do with the labour trouble. There were troops in Winnipeg at the time. They were never used.
