I know nothing of the incident to which my hon. friend refers. I am glad my hon. friend did not make a personal reference to me, because I do not know where his farm is; all I know is that he represents Marquette in this House. I was saying that workers do not go lightly on strike.
Answer the question.

A little detail as to what
goes on does not matter very much. This clearly indicates, as I have just stated, that some hon. gentlemen who make statements in this House do not really understand what Labour stands for or they would not ask a question of that kind: Why did somebody come on my farm and ask the workers to go off? The question is absurd in regard to a strike of 30,000 workers. Does anyone think that everybody who has anything to do with a strike knows all the little details that happen at such a time?
I was referring to an incident in 1918 when there was a strike in Winnipeg. During that time I did my best to try to settle the strike. I was a member of the city council at that time. What happened to me? I was condemned from both sides. On the one hand the workers and on the other the city council condemned me because I tried to settle it. That is often what happens to the peacemaker during a strike and consequently I am not very anxious to act as a peacemaker when a strike occurs.
When the strike of 1919 took place I saw that the workers were right and I gave them my unflinching support on that occasion. There is no doubt about their being right; no worker goes on strike except as a last resort and when compelled to do so by force of circumstances. But what I protest and will always protest against is when a government, I care not which party it is, attempts to suppress by forcible methods, what should after all be the inalienable right of every Canadian citizen.
On that particular morning of June 17 those eight or ten men were arrested and sent to Stony Mountain penitentiary, the idea being to deport them. Those men were arrested not because of their participation in the strike because some of them had hardly participated in it at all, had no part in calling it, and had come into Winnipeg more or less accidentally. Those men were arrested and were to be deported because they had certain ideas which were distasteful to the powers that be. The men were selected for deportation at the ' instigation of the then government and the man who did the selection was the then Minister of Labour. The documents will go to prove that if they are ever brought down to the House.
I am sorry if I have detained the House so long as I have; this matter has come up rather unexpectedly to-night. Personally, I do not care to look backward; I prefer to look forward. _
Hear, hear.
I wish some hon. gentlemen who sit on the other side would also look a little forward and not always look backward. Looking backward is generally a prerogative of the legal profession.
If the hon. gentleman would keep to his own field, it would perhaps be better all round.

I once had nine months' experience of law and somebody said that I would have made a pretty good lawyer if I had stayed at it' a little longer. I had quite an experience of lawyers and one thing that was taught me was that lawyers knew nothing about law; that the only man who knew law was the judge; that what the judge said was law and what a lawyer said was merely an opinion and nothing more. After seeing lawyers in action for a short period I said

that I would have nothing to do with them; that I was going to plead my own case. I did so and I happened to be the only one who was unlucky or lucky enough to be acquitted.
If I may I will pursue the story a little further as it is worth repeating. A few weeks after the trials were over I met the late Judge Metcalfe on Portage Avenue in the city of Winnipeg and after the usual saluta-tations he said: " Heaps, the luckiest thing in the world for you was that you had no lawyer defending you. If you had had a lawyer to defend you, you would have gone to gaol with the rest." Ever since then I have had an idea that when we take notice of lawyers as we sometimes do in this House we always get into all kinds of trouble. If you wish to keep out of trouble in this House or out of it do not take too much notice of what lawyers say. Lawyers as a rule can go back for precedents for thousands of years, but when it comes to looking forward for five or ten minutes they sometimes get hopelessly lost.
I wish however to impress upon hon. members again that when a strike takes place we should bear in mind that as was the case with those men in the city of Winnipeg, the men are as good and loyal Canadians as you have in the Dominion of Canada. In the Winnipeg strike thousands of those men had just come back from overseas. To-day they are in the ranks of the organized labour movement, and they were in the ranks of the organized labour movement in 1919.
Was the hon. member one of them?

I frankly admit that I did not go overseas. If loyalty, if patriotism is to be determined by a man's desire and 'inclination for war I am no patriot. If patriotism means love of your people and of your country I am second to nobody in this House or outside of it.
Well, well.

If the hon. gentleman wants to interrupt me in an orderly way I hope he will get up and do so. The strike in Winnipeg took place; it is gone; it is a thing of the past. I would say to those gentlemen who were in charge of events of that period that if they had only had the same feeling, perhaps even the same amount of understanding as has the Prime Minister of Great Britain at the present time, those events would never have taken place in Winnipeg
1919. There was a desire at that time to crush organized labour.
Is the hon. gentleman in order at the present time?
Yes.

I do not know whether the hon. member is a lawyer or not. I was saying that if the members of the House of 1919 had had the same breadth of outlook, the same understanding as the Prime Minister of Great Britain has at the present time those events in Winnipeg in 1919 might have been spared. Nevertheless, in spite of what took place there organized labour can never be crushed. The more attempts that are made to crush organized labour, the stronger it will rise. The organized labour movement is never defeated. It may lose here or it may lose there, but ultimately it will come back stronger than ever.

Mr. Speaker, I shall not take many
minutes of the time of the House in regard to this matter. The hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) has made certain statements to which I wish to refer. He informed us that he was not afraid of facts, and for that we shall all be devoutly grateful. I couple with that the statement he made a little later that he hoped with some experience to conduct himself with a little more accuracy than he was able to do now. Wre can put the two together and draw our own conclusions. The hon. gentleman says that in Winnipeg no children had to suffer for want of milk. He did not answer the question I put to him: did the strike committee cut off the delivery of bread and milk? That question he sidestepped; he declined to answer it. I want therefore to read to this hon. gentleman, who is not afraid of facts, what was stated in the bulletin issued by the strike committee, of which I suppose he was a member. He declares that he was deeply involved in the whole thing, and certainly his sympathies were with the undertaking. This is the bulletin issued by the committee on May 17 with reference to their proposal to establish supply depots to give preference to strike families.
Impossible to distinguish between the sick children owing to the fact that it would take days to establish a card system and reports fast coming in of children on verge of death for the want of milk.
So that some of them did have sufficient compassion, when they saw children on the verge of death for the want of the very necessaries of life, to withdraw that order which they had issued and which they had proposed to carry out, giving preference to the families of those who were engaged in the strike and withholding any consideration

from those who did not participate in it. That is the situation which the hon. gentleman has described as a quiet, peaceable strike. The fact is that the Winnipeg disturbance was not an ordinary strike, the object of which was to obtain better wages. It was an organized attempt to get control of the city and to induce labour in other centres of population to do likewise, with the end in view of destroying or breaking down national government. I do not think I can do better than quote some of the utterances of the hon. member and others associated with him on that occasion, and in the first place I might read what was said by the hon. member sitting immediately to his left (Mr. Woodsworth). Speaking in Vancouver on February 7 of that year that gentleman said:
The ultimate object of the Federated Labour Party is the collective ownership and democratic operation of the means of wealth production. This involves a complete revolution in our whole economic and social structure.
That is from one of the leaders in this movement. Let me quote again from the same source:
The federal authorities control the military and the courts, and labour is not going to get what it wants until it in some way gets control of the military and the courts.
That is the peaceable strike. That is the spirit that moved this very quiet and law abiding demonstration on the part of labour. Now I will quote from another gentleman who was prominent in the movement, a Mr. Russell:
The blood that is spilled in Canada will depend on the working class. We must establish the same form of government as they have in Russia so that we may have a Russian democracy here.
That is what that prominent participant in the strike declared at that time, and I have heard somewhat similar opinions expressed since then.
* The hon. member who resumed his seat a moment ago (Mr. Heaps) criticized the act which was put through this parliament on that occasion for the deportation of undesirable people, and he observed that it had been disposed of in twenty minutes. That act, Mr. Speaker, was adopted unanimously, not a single voice having been raised in dissent. All I have to say to the hon. gentleman is that the people of this country, regardless of their political affiliations, welcome to Canada decent, law abiding men and women, no matter from what country they may come. But I want him to understand-and he can convey this message to those who think and feel as he does in matters of this kind- that the Canadian people, upon whom depends the future stability of this country, 14011-255
will not tolerate foreigners who come to these shores imbued with the determination to stir up trouble. We will not permit such people to come and establish on the soil of Canada conditions of the sort from which they were running away in leaving the country of their origin.
This was a peaceable strike, says the hon. member for North Winnipeg. Let us see what he himself said at the time. Speaking in July of that year he expressed this regret:
We were having beautiful weather and we were having a beautiful strike when the citizens butted into the game and began to attempt to assert their authority.
A terrible thing for the law abiding citizens of Winnipeg to interfere with that beautiful strike, during such beautiful weather.

Another evidence of the kindly disposition of the gentlemen associated with the hon. member for North Winnipeg and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

The hon.
gentleman may suggest what he likes. I have not been so close to the treasury benches as he has been, this session at all events, and I have not been able to dictate any of the terms of the Speech from the Throne. I will give the House another quotation.

With his permission I
would ask the hon. member this question: In view of the past attitude of the hon. member for North Winnipeg and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre with regard to labour, why does he classify those hon. gentlemen as belonging to the Labour party?

I am not
the first man who has found it difficult to answer a question on the spur of the moment. It would be rather hard for me to give a sound reason for classifying these hon. gentlemen as representatives of labour, and I must say I appreciate the point raised by my hon. friend from Renfrew (Mr. Maloney). In all earnestness and sincerity, however, I am bound to confess that hon. gentlemen across the way, representing the city of Winnipeg, notwithstanding that they classify themselves as Labour members, are not in my opinion, in any true sense of the word, real representatives of Labour and of labour interests in this country.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, speaking at Calgary on October 29 of that year, said:
I am not worrying as to whether 'they keep me in the pen or not-we'Ll win anyway. I don't think the workers of .this country will let us stay in anyway.
The hon. gentleman had at any rate the consolation of believing that, even though the utterances of himself and of his associates did create turmoil and result in his landing behind the doors of a penitentiary, he had a sufficient number of friends outside who would use their influence and endeavour to get him out. He would not stay in very long.
The Winnipeg strike, Mr. Speaker, was not an ordinary strike in any sense of the term. I repeat, after the most careful consideration of the matter, that I have no hesitation in asserting that it was a deliberate attempt on the part of certain persons to get control of the city and to induce labour in other centres of population to follow their lead, with the ultimate object of overthrowing the properly

constituted government of this country and establishing in its place something along the lines that one of those strike leaders expressed himself so much in favour of, namely, "what they had in Russia"-the most debased country to-day on the face of the globe.
I repeat what I said' a few moments ago, Sir, that we are all sympathetic towards Labour. We recognize that Labour is entitled to demand its rights. We welcome people from all countries of the world to come here and establish their homes, but it is just as well for certain hon. gentlemen who sit opposite to thoroughly understand, and convey that understanding to those with whom they were associated in bringing about the Winnipeg strike, that we Canadians do not propose to allow men to come into this country from Europe or any other part of the world and establish conditions such as drove them out of their native land.

Hear, hear.

Again I ask
a question similar to the question I asked on a somewhat like occasion:	To what purpose
is the time of this House taken up with the discussion of the strike in the city of Winnipeg some seven years ago? I tell you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members, that it is for one purpose only-propaganda pure and simple.
I go further. I trust too much to the intelligence of this House to suggest that it * will be misled by the speech of the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) into believing that in speaking as he has tonight he is representing or forwarding in any substantial way the interests of honest, sane labour in the Dominion. He has told you that the late Minister of Labour, now Senator Robertson, dare not come into the city of Winnipeg to address a public meeting, if public announcements thereof were properly made. I now tell him that during the last federal election the same Senator Robertson did come to the city of Winnipeg and did there address public meetings that were publicly advertised with his name at the top of the list in my constituency, and at no

meeting that he addressed did he receive to my knowledge one single interruption, but on the contrary he was accorded most attentive and enthusiastic hearings.
As evidence of how labour stands in the constituency of Winnipeg South Centre let me refer to the result of the last general election.	I may say, without any lack of
modesty, that in my opinion Winnipeg South Centre is a very important constituency and in point of population and of the number of registered electors is in fact the greatest constituency west of the lakes. During the recent election a candidate of his party-the Independent Labour party-contested that constituency and lost his deposit. Senator Robertson addressed several meetings during the course of the contest. I do not give him credit entirely for the result, I take some credit to myself, with the loyal support of the rank and file of that constituency. But I want to tell the hon. member for North Winnipeg that the constituency of Winnipeg South Centre has among its electorate far and above any other class of people the labouring class, and yet the candidate representing the Independent Labour party was out of the running entirely in fifty out of the fifty-two polls, and in the aggregate, as I have said, he lost his deposit. I merely cite that to show to this House that so far as Winnipeg is concerned hon. gentlemen do not need to worry as to what real Labour will do there. If the House has any apprehension as to the status of Labour in that city, I now declare there is no cause for alarm. The 1919 strike was taken care of not by the militia, but by the citizens at large; and I can assure hon. members that in the event of any strikes in the future similar to that of 1919 they will be taken care of again by the same citizens.
The hon. member for North Winnipeg has told us that he prefers to look forward rather than backward. Well, I ask this House:	Which way has he been looking to-night? Has he been taking a forward view? Rather has he been stirring up these unpleasant memories of the past. I ask for what purpose. I submit that it is only for the purpose of serving the individual ends of the hon. member himself. His purpose, in season and out of season, of which the House has had a good demonstration tonight, is not to solve the problems of labour in this country but to stir up dissension and discord in order that he may thereby profit.

Now, the hon. gentleman has referred to the conditions in the city of Winnipeg during the strike. I myself have a very distinct, recollection of those conditions-11 p.m. In the early part of June 1919 I returned to Winnipeg with a regiment that is well known to many hon. members of the west-the 46th battalion. That is a battalion of which Saskatchewan has a right to be proud. Because of the strike conditions we were unable to get telegrams to our families advising them of our return. The street car service was suspended. Milk was allowed to be delivered to homes only by those whose dairy wagons bore the card, "Operated by permission of the strike committee." Restaurant keepers were intimidated, and many of them found it to their advantage to post in their windows cards bearing the inscription "Kept open by permission of the strike committee," or an inscription to the like effect. Fire protection in the city of Winnipeg, as an effective protection, was cut off. Police protection was interfered with. Fire protection was demoralized to such an extent that it was necessary for the civilians to go into the fire halls and take the place of the men who were called out in order that the homes of the citizens of Winnipeg might be protected. So far as police protection was concerned, a much similar condition prevailed. Citizens of Winnipeg had to be sworn in as special constables to protect their own homes and their property. The first night that I arrived home and went to my house I was asked by my neighbours to come out and discuss the situation as to the protection of property, and I tell the House this:	We went to the end
of the street and met on a little lot, and there arranged for patrols in order that the street might be patroled from sunset to sunrise to protect property. Hon. gentlemen may say that our fears were groundless, but I tell you, Mr. Speaker, and the members of this House, that that was the condition of mind of the people of the city of Winnipeg at that time. That is what the hon. member (Mr. Heaps) refers to as a peaceful strike.
Let me say this: So far as Labour is concerned, Labour will never find me its enemy in this House or outside of it. I believe in a fair wage. I believe in fair living conditions. I believe in the right of Labour to organize to advance its interests. But when agitators seek to use unionism in labour, not to advance but to prostitute the cause of Labour, I hay it is time to call a halt. That was the condition which existed in Winnipeg in 1919 due-

ing the strike referred to this evening. That has passed. It was dealt with by the citizens of Winnipeg, and perhaps the less said about it the better.
The hon. member for North Winnipeg has made same references to patriotism. He has told you that it is not necessary to be in favour of war in order to be a patriot; I agree. But there are some things, whether you call it patriotism or not, that are expected of a citizen of a country. I think we cannot place the duties of even the humblest citizen of Canlada lower than this, that we have a right to expect of him that he shall uphold the laws for the time being of his country, and that if he seeks to bring about a change, he shall do so only by constitutional means. I submit that the test I have given is not too strong a test. Measuring the hon. member for North Winnipeg by that test, I leave it to this House to judge how high he stands. If there be any doubt, I would like to refer to the House an extract that has been handed to me, and to read it and ask the hon. member whether he is the person referred to in this article. Winnipeg, Man., May 1.-Instructions of chief of police Newton that a Union Jack be placed at the head of the column was the only hitdh in to-day's May day parade. This part of special interest:
After the parade a mass meeting was held, presided over by Aid. A. A. Heaps. The Union Jack was th^n deposited beneath the rostrum and the red banner hoisted.
Is that the test by which patriotism shall be measured in this country? Judge for yourselves the patriotism of the hon. member.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say this: While this demonstration in the House to-night on the part of the hon. member for North Winnipeg may be something of a novelty here, it is no novelty to us in the city of Winnipeg. We understand it there, and it is so that you may properly appreciate it, that I rise to-night. as have been expressed here to-night by him do not represent Labour in the city of Winnipeg. Let me say further that during the last federal campaign organized Labour in the city of Winnipeg was not behind the Independent Labour party.

1.	We believe that Braun never visited the Red Lake district, as he states he did-and further states, that he remained in the district ninety days-basing our belief upon an affidavit made by Capt. A. S. Stevens, of Cobalt, that Braun made declaration to him that he had not been in the district, but had a representative there.
2.	No man has driven into the district with eleven dogs as he states he did, and no man could leave the district in the dead of winter via aeroplane without the authorities having knowledge of this fact.
3.	None of the undersigned ever heard of him, and there is no record, as evidenced by inquiries made through Mr. Joe Kenneally, that he was ever in the district, and no one ever saw him, or heard of him, until they read the articles above referred to.
There are hardships to be borne by the pioneers who go into a new country, and Red Lake is no exception to this experience, but none of the hardships as portrayed in his articles. There is no shortage of food, and with the breaking up of winter and the opening up of water transportation there will be assured shipments that will meet the demand of the men who are now there and of those who will go into the district this year. The properly constituted authorities have not and will not delegate their responsibilities for the welfare and safety of those who prospect and mine in the north country.
His false and ignorant statements regarding the geological and economic conditions in Red Lake district stamp him as totally unreliable and devoid of character or knowledge, and how the statements of such a man can be accepted and published by resDonsible

We are 'basing our activities upon the findings of expert opinion, both official and private, and upon a wide experience in the important work of prospecting a country for economic deposits of ore, which will increase the wealth of the province and the Dominion, and resent keenly the reflection upon the character and integrity of the men who have devoted their Lives to this great industry, and more especially through the inference that there is no protection and that there has been no effort upon the part of the proper authorities to safeguard in every way possible the interests of those who are interested An mining in northern Ontario.

When you try to realize, Mr. Speaker, what a producing mining area, particularly at this location, will mean to our great railway systems, to the country as a whole, and parti cularly to the vicinity of Winnipeg, which has come in for so much adverse criticism to-night, I feel quite justified in taking advantage of the publicity following a statement in this House. I feel that the men in the north country have every justification in being incensed at any attempt to malign their efforts or to defame this wonderfully promising area. Besides, there are hundreds of intrepid prospectors, the noblest and pluckiest fellows in the world, braving the elements, risking their lives and spending their all, drawn on by some inscrutable and irresistible impulse, year in and year out, in the interests of mining which means so much to mankind, and it is easy to imagine how they resent the lying criticism of a mercenary and misinformed charlatan.

We need capital to open up our country and to develop our natural resources. Every man in the north country welcomes United States capital. I know all hon. members will agree with me when I say that every effort should be made by the federal and provincial authorities to see that capital will receive just protection and encouragement in Canada. Braun's statements bear the opposite implication and should be refuted from every angle. For the sake of international courtesy and good-will, I trust the press will give similar publicity to this disclaimer as to the meretricious fabrications of this gypsy geologist.

The hon. member for North Timiskaming (Mr. O'Neill) asked me as coming from, northern Ontario to give him some support in the remarks which he has just made. I am pleased to do so in view of the fact that that great section of northern Ontario has, I think, been slandered by this man Braun. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) who acts as Minister of Mines, is not in his seat, and I should like to draw to his attention the remarks of the hon. member for North Timiskaming. No doubt the Department of Mines has reports upon the Red Lake district which, according to the statement of my 'hon. friend, has been slandered, and I am sure those reports would show that the statements of this man Braun are gross exaggerations and slanders upon that district. It is in the interest of the Dominion of Canada that statements such as Braun has made should not go unchallenged, and I believe the Minister of Mines would be well advised if he looked or had one of his officials look into them and if possible issue an official statement from the department as to the facts of the case. I hope the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), who is leading the House at the moment, will draw to the attention of the Minister of the Interior the statements made by the hon. member for North Timiskaming.

speechtext: Certainly.

Last week and this week in Toronto I came in touch with the Mines Department of Ontario and they are most encouraged at headquarters by the reports they receive as to the coming development not only in northern Ontario, and Manitoba, but all round that country. My feeling-and I think it is more or less correct -is that from now on we shall see in this country a mining exploration and development almost unequalled in the history of the world. It will not be confined to one province, but
